concept.shortExplanation: A model with enough capacity can drive its training error to zero by memorising the noise, and that is the failure mode that looks most like success. The only honest signal is performance on data the fit never saw. Regularisation works by making large weights expensive, so the fit has to justify complexity with real signal. The polynomial fits here are solved by real least squares with a ridge penalty, recomputed every time you move a control.
concept.ahaMoment: Training loss went down the whole time. It went down while the model got worse. Any metric computed on the data you fitted is incapable of telling you when to stop.

levels.title: Pick the Degree
levels.instructions: Raise the polynomial degree and watch training loss fall while validation loss turns around. Stop at the degree that generalises best.
hints: Start at degree 1 and slowly raise it — training loss will keep falling the whole way, but validation loss will fall for a while and then start climbing back up. The turning point is your answer, not the degree with the lowest training loss.
This data was generated from a genuine cubic curve. Once the degree can express a cubic, more capacity stops helping and starts hunting for patterns in the noise instead.
Degree 3 is the turning point — validation loss bottoms out there around 0.044, comfortably past three stars. Degrees 4–6 are still fine (~0.07); by degree 7 it's already overfitting.

levels.title: Tame Degree Twelve
levels.instructions: The degree is locked at twelve — far more capacity than this data deserves. Use the ridge penalty alone to bring validation loss back down without touching the degree.
hints: Degree is locked at 12 — far more flexible than this data needs — so at λ=0 it memorises the noise. Raise λ and watch validation loss fall even as training loss rises.

There's a wide range of λ that works here, not one exact value. Push it up past roughly 0.5 and validation loss keeps improving, well past the point where training loss starts looking 'worse' on its own.
λ ≈ 1.0 brings validation loss down to about 0.061, safely inside three stars — degree 12 does not need to be dialed back, only made expensive to use carelessly.

levels.title: Close the Gap
levels.instructions: Noisier data, fewer samples. Tune both degree and penalty to minimise the gap between training and validation loss while keeping the fit useful.
hints: You have two dials now — degree and λ — and the goal is a small gap, not just a small validation loss on its own. A flat, useless line also has a 'small gap' in a hollow sense, which is exactly what this level's validation-loss ceiling exists to rule out.

This data comes from a sine curve, and the sample here is smaller and noisier than the last level's. A moderate degree flexible enough to bend like a sine, with a modest ridge penalty to keep it honest, closes the gap without flattening the fit into uselessness.

Degree 3 with λ = 0 already gets you there — gap of about 0.02, comfortably inside three stars, with validation loss (~0.054) nowhere near the 0.1 ceiling. Degree 6 with λ around 0.3–0.5 works just as well if you want more flexibility with some insurance against it.
